name: Meaningful Match Cut
source_tutorial: transcripts/what not to do in editing.txt
use_when: Two shots share shape, motion, position, or action and the connection adds meaning.
The cut can compress time, compare ideas, show evolution, or create a deliberate conceptual link.
A visual match supports the spoken point rather than distracting from it.
avoid_when: The match exists only to show editing skill.
The match implies a false or offensive relationship between subjects.
The spoken point needs a simple illustrative shot more than a clever transition.

timeline_pattern.meaning_rule: The audience should understand why the two images were connected.
timeline_pattern.implication_rule: Check what the cut says by placing subject A next to subject B.

motion.rule: Match motion, shape, or screen position only when the conceptual link is desired.
motion.avoid: Accidental head-turn, gesture, or shape matches that compare unrelated people or ideas.

sound.rule: Sound can bridge a match cut, but should not make an accidental implication feel intentional.

captions.rule: Captions should clarify the intended comparison if the visual match could be misread.

color.rule: Color similarity can strengthen the match, but should not override meaning.

implementation.ffmpeg: Generate before/after frames around match candidates and review the implied relationship before rendering.
implementation.remotion: Use explicit metadata for match target, match source, and intended meaning before animating the transition.
implementation.blender: Use match cuts in animation only when the object transformation or comparison advances the story.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Avoid template match transitions unless the two shots have a story relationship.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Use markers on both matched frames and write the intended meaning in sequence notes.

common_mistakes: Making a match cut because it looks cool.
Distracting from the narration with a clever transition.
Accidentally comparing the speaker to a villain, oppressor, or unrelated subject.
Ignoring the meaning created by shot adjacency.
qc: Can the editor state the meaning of the match cut?
Does the cut support the narration or story point?
Could the adjacency imply something offensive or false?
Would a simple cut communicate the idea better?
